items.question: The 19th-century socio-religious reform movements are often described as the 'Indian Renaissance'. Examine their character and assess their contribution to social awakening and Indian nationalism.
items.modelAnswer: The **19th-century socio-religious reform movements** arose when Indian society was weighed down by **Sati, child marriage, female infanticide, untouchability and caste rigidity**, and when **Western education, liberal ideas and a critique of colonial exploitation** stirred an educated middle class to act. Their **twin character** combined **religious reform** — attacking idolatry, superstition and priestly monopoly, and returning to 'pure' scripture (Ram Mohan Roy's monotheistic **Brahmo Samaj**, 1828; Dayananda's **Arya Samaj**, 1875, 'back to the Vedas') — with **social reform**, targeting evils against women and lower castes. Concrete gains followed: the **abolition of Sati (1829)**, the **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (1856)** under **Vidyasagar**, and the **Age of Consent Act (1891)** through **Malabari**. Reform cut across communities — the **Aligarh Movement** (Sir Syed Ahmad Khan) among Muslims, the **Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha** among Parsis, and the **Singh Sabha** among Sikhs — while **Jyotirao Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj** and **Sree Narayana Guru's SNDP** attacked caste itself. Yet the movements had **limits**: many were **elite and urban**, sometimes **revivalist** and internally divisive along communal lines. On balance, by reviving **rational inquiry and cultural pride** and forging a **collective identity**, they earned the label 'Indian Renaissance' and **laid the social foundation of the nationalist movement**.
keyPoints: Context: Sati, child marriage, untouchability, caste rigidity; stimuli were Western education and liberal/revolutionary ideas.
Twin character: religious reform (anti-idolatry, back-to-scripture) + social reform (women and caste uplift).
Legislative gains: Sati abolition (1829), Widows' Remarriage Act (1856), Age of Consent Act (1891).
Cross-community spread: Brahmo/Arya Samaj, Aligarh, Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha, Singh Sabha, Satyashodhak, SNDP.
Limits: elite/urban base, revivalist tendencies, occasional communal division.
Legacy: rational awakening and collective identity that fed Indian nationalism ('Indian Renaissance').
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Modern History: Socio-Religious Reform Movements

items.question: Assess the contribution of Kandukuri Veeresalingam and his contemporaries to social reform and the Telugu cultural renaissance in the Andhra region.
items.modelAnswer: The **Andhra reform movement** of the late 19th and early 20th centuries fused **social reform** with a **Telugu literary and linguistic renaissance**, and its towering figure was **Kandukuri Veeresalingam (1848–1919)**, rightly called the **father of the Telugu Renaissance**. Drawing on **Brahmo Samaj** ideals, he organised the **first widow remarriage in the Telugu region at Rajahmundry (1881)**, fought **dowry, child marriage and the nautch (devadasi) system**, opened **schools for girls**, edited the reformist journal ***Vivekavardhini***, and wrote ***Rajasekhara Charitramu***, an early Telugu social novel that turned literature into a vehicle of reform. His contemporaries widened this awakening: **Gurajada Apparao (1862–1915)** wrote ***Kanyasulkam*** (1892), the first modern Telugu play, satirising the sale of young girls in marriage, and championed **spoken (vaaduka) Telugu** and patriotic verse (*Desamunu Preminchumanna*). **Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu (1862–1939)**, a leading **Brahmo Samaj** reformer and educationist, led the **anti-nautch** and **social-purity/temperance** campaigns. **Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy (1863–1940)** carried the linguistic reform forward through the **Vyavaharika Bhasha (spoken-Telugu) movement** against classical Grandhika, and studied the **Savara tribal language** — his birthday, **29 August, is now Telugu Language Day**. Together they **modernised Telugu society and its language**, making Andhra a vibrant centre of the wider Indian Renaissance and preparing the ground for its nationalist and self-respect currents.
keyPoints: Kandukuri Veeresalingam: father of the Telugu Renaissance; first Telugu-region widow remarriage (Rajahmundry, 1881); anti-dowry/child-marriage/nautch; Vivekavardhini; Rajasekhara Charitramu; Brahmo ideals.
Gurajada Apparao: Kanyasulkam (1892) against bride-price/child marriage; champion of spoken Telugu; Desamunu Preminchumanna.
Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu: Brahmo Samaj reformer and educationist; anti-nautch and social-purity/temperance movements.
Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy: Vyavaharika Bhasha (spoken-Telugu) movement; study of Savara; 29 August is Telugu Language Day.
Combined effect: modernised both Telugu society and language, embedding Andhra in the Indian Renaissance.
items.source: standard references on Andhra social reformers (Veeresalingam, Gurajada, Naidu, Gidugu)
